sections.title: Astrology
sections.html:
Astrology is a system based on the belief that the stars and constellations moving in their orbits in the heavens influence everything that happens in the world, because life, with its good and its bad, flows from on high through the position of the stars and constellations. The stars (kokhavim) are the seven heavenly bodies that were considered planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Ḥama (the sun), Venus, Mercury and the moon (whose Hebrew initials form the mnemonic "Shatzam Ḥanakhal"). The constellations (mazalot) are twelve groups of distant stars that form shapes, as it were, in the sky, after which they are named: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces. Since the heavenly bodies move in their orbits, their influence changes at every moment according to the position of the stars and constellations: each month has its own constellation, and each day and hour has its own arrangement of stars, and according to the combination between them, astrologers draw up a person's birth chart and foretell his fate. Likewise with regard to the fate of nations and countries: according to the position of the stars at the time of their founding, or at the time of important events that happened to them, they determine what events, opportunities or difficulties await them in the future.

For thousands of years the sciences of astronomy and astrology were intertwined, and the sages of the nations of the world, including the sages of Babylonia, Assyria, Egypt and Greece, believed in astrology. In the course of time, sages arose who challenged the reliability of astrology, until, through a gradual process, a clear division was formed between the two. Astronomy developed as an exact science that advances with the help of sophisticated telescopes, through which one can see distant stars, star systems and galaxies, and on the basis of observing them one can calculate their orbits and the gravitational forces acting on them. Astrology, by contrast, is a system that its believers have not managed to prove scientifically, and therefore many hold that there is no truth in it.

In general, in the days of the Talmud, when there was a general consensus among the sages of the nations of the world that astrology is a true science, the Sages of Israel did not dispute them. The Talmud (Shabbat 119a) even brings stories that rest on this conception, such as the story of "Yosef who honours the Sabbath," who lived in a place where there also lived a gentile who owned much property. The Chaldeans (stargazers) told that gentile that all his property would fall into the hands of Yosef. The gentile wished to prevent this, sold all his property, bought a precious pearl with the proceeds and hid it in his hat. As he crossed a river, a wind blew and sent his hat flying into the water, and a large fish swallowed the pearl. Some time later that fish was caught and brought to the market close to the onset of Shabbat. Since everyone had already bought their Shabbat needs, no buyer could be found for it. The fishermen said: presumably Yosef who honours the Sabbath, who is accustomed to go out of his way to buy every good food in honour of Shabbat, will want to buy it. They brought him the fish, and he bought it. When he opened the fish, he found the pearl. He sold it for an enormous sum and became rich.

In the days of the Rishonim, when among the sages of the nations of the world there were already those who held that the system of astrology was mistaken, there were also among the Sages of Israel those who held so (see below, note 1). One should not be surprised that the Sages of Israel take the sages of the nations of the world into account, for Torah scholars do not presume to decide scientific questions on the basis of the Torah, because the aim of the Torah is to teach us the most important things: what is good and what is bad, what is forbidden and what is permitted, and not to decide scientific questions.

sections.title: Explaining the Debate over the Status of Astrology
sections.html:
One can explain that in principle there is truth in astrology. For just as the Lord created all creatures, each with its own uniqueness, so He created time, each time with its own uniqueness; and it stands to reason that creatures that appeared at a certain time are influenced by the special character of that time. Moreover, since all creatures in the world are connected to one another, one can in principle learn from one system about another, and especially from a system that encompasses the world, such as the stars of the heavens. However, since the position of the stars is very complex, it is difficult to establish a clear forecast according to them, for a person's birth chart is composed of three factors – hour, day and month – each of which is complex in itself. In addition, the fate of every person depends on the fate of his family members, his friends, the people of his city and his nation, and it is not possible to draw up astrological charts for all the people, families, societies and nations. And even if it were possible, the human mind cannot calculate them all together while knowing which chart has more influence.

Apparently, the successful astrologers were multidisciplinary sages who delved deeply into the individual soul and understood social processes, and were also endowed with a mystical talent, with whose help they could identify, from the totality of the data in the astrological chart, the principal components, and receive inspiration to foretell the future. And although they were not infrequently mistaken, since there were no better tools to help people and rulers plan their moves for the future, many relied on their forecasts.

As systematic science developed, the demand for precision grew, and since the astrologers could not be precise, their wisdom was cast into doubt, and talented people preferred to develop their talent in a scientific direction at the expense of mystical talent. Thus the people capable of foretelling the future with the help of astrology dwindled. As a result, the tradition of transmitting this wisdom was also damaged, until over time the sages able, with the help of astrology, to understand a person's character and inclinations became few, and all the more so there is almost no one able to foretell the future by means of it.

It emerges, then, that those who hold that there is truth in astrology relied on the cases in which astrologers succeeded in foretelling the future. Those who hold that it is false, by contrast, demanded higher rates of prediction, which it cannot meet, especially in generations in which the best talent was directed to exact science at the expense of developing the mystical sense.1

sections.title: The Position of the Sages of Israel
sections.html:
As stated, at the time when the sages of the world agreed that astrology is a true science, the Sages of Israel did not dispute them; however, on the basis of the faith of Israel they emphasised several principles which changed the attitude towards it at its root, and thereby prevented the danger that it would influence Israel for the bad. First, in contrast to the idolaters, who held that the stars are what influence what happens in the world, the Sages of Israel explained that the stars and constellations too are created beings, and they only reflect the fate that the Lord has determined; consequently, by the will of the Lord the mazal will change. They further said that even the most talented astrologers will not succeed in foretelling the future precisely, for the Lord gave man free choice, and by his good or bad deeds he can change his fate. This applies especially to Israel, who received the Torah and the mitzvot, through which they can rise above the stars and constellations and rectify themselves and the whole world; and conversely, if they choose evil, they will be punished more. Therefore, according to most of the Sages (Shabbat 156a-b): "Israel is not subject to mazal" (ein mazal le-Yisrael); that is, the astrological charts that foresee the fortune of Israel are not decisive, and they are able to change their fate by their choices and their deeds (see the next halakha).

Likewise the Amora Rav said (ibid.) that after the Lord chose Avraham our father to establish the people of Israel from his offspring, Avraham our father turned to the Holy One, blessed be He, and said: "Master of the Universe, I have looked into my astrology (my astrological chart), and I am not fit to father a son! He said to him: Go out from your astrology, for Israel is not subject to mazal." For what did you see? That the planet Jupiter is in the west and therefore you cannot father children? Behold, I am moving it to the east, and you can father children. Similarly, the Sages said (Bereshit Rabba 44:10) that Avraham our father said before the Master of the Universe: My mazal presses me, so that I cannot father children. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Indeed, "Avram" and "Sarai" cannot father children, but since I have changed your names to "Avraham" and "Sara," you can father children.

Likewise, the Sages said (Sota 12b) of the stargazers that they "see but do not know what they see, utter but do not know what they utter." Pharaoh's seers foresaw that the saviour of Israel was about to be born and that he was destined to be stricken through water; Pharaoh therefore decreed (Shemot 1:22): "Every son that is born you shall cast into the river." Since Moshe was placed in an ark in the river, the sign disappeared, and they thought that he had already been stricken and died, and they annulled the decree; they did not understand that what they had seen was that Moshe was destined to be stricken over the "waters of Meriva," and because of this he would not enter the Land.

Similarly, the Sages related (Shabbat 156b) that the Amora Shmuel was sitting with Ablet, who was a gentile sage and stargazer. People passed before them on their way to cut reeds near a lake. Ablet pointed at one of the men and said: "This man will go and not return; a snake will bite him and he will die." Shmuel said to him: "If he is a Jew, he will go and return." While they were sitting, that man returned from the lake. Ablet rose to examine his load and found in it a dead snake cut into two pieces. It turned out that he had indeed foreseen correctly that a snake would come upon him, but instead of the snake killing the man, the snake died. Shmuel asked the man: What did you do today? He related that he had performed an act of charity with a companion who had nothing to eat, and had given him of his own in a way that would not embarrass him. It emerges that by virtue of the mitzva he performed, his fate was changed from death to life.

They further related (Shabbat 156b) concerning the daughter of Rabbi Akiva that the stargazers foresaw that on her wedding day a snake would bite her and she would die. Rabbi Akiva was very worried about this, but he did not refrain from marrying her off. When she went to her home on her wedding night, she removed an ornamented pin from her hair and placed it in a hole in the wall. In the morning she took the pin and saw that a dead snake was dragged along after it. It turned out that during the night she had stuck it into the snake's eye. Rabbi Akiva asked his daughter: What good deed did you do on the wedding day by virtue of which you were saved? She related that towards evening a poor man called out at the door of the house, and no one heard him because everyone was busy with the wedding feast; but she heard him, took her own portion and gave it to him. Rabbi Akiva said: You performed a mitzva, and it is what saved you from death.

It emerges, then, that the Sages brought stories in which the astrologers foresaw correctly, yet in practice they were not right, because Israel is above mazal, and with the help of the Torah and the mitzvot they change the mazal. Thus the Sages taught us that one should not consult astrologers, but should cleave to the path of the Torah and the mitzvot, and thereby merit life and blessing. In the course of this we learned how the Sages of Israel, on the one hand, respect the sages of the nations of the world and make use of their wisdom, and on the other hand, on the basis of the foundations of the faith of Israel, remove the moral damage that could be caused by their positions.

sections.title: The Relationship between Mazal-Fate and Human Deeds
sections.html:
The Sages disagreed (Shabbat 156a) on the question of whether "Israel is subject to mazal" – that is, whether the normal situation for Israel is that mazal is decisive, and only rarely does it change, or whether the normal situation for Israel is that mazal is flexible and open to change. The question also concerns the proper way for a Jew to conduct himself in the face of the difficulties and obstacles that stand before him: whether it is proper to act within the framework of his mazal without exerting himself too much to change it, because only rarely does it change; or whether it is proper for him to strive, through good deeds and prayers, to try to change his mazal.

This question does not depend on one's position towards astrology, for instead of "mazal" one can speak of "fate," which depends on three factors: a) The genes, which determine his talent, his psychological tendencies, his appearance, his health and his susceptibility to certain illnesses. b) The environment into which he was born, which greatly influences his ability to develop his talents. One who is born into a family of righteous people or of criminals, of rich or of poor, of learned or of ignorant people, in a period of prosperity or a period of war or famine, into a poor and oppressed nation or a rich and successful nation, is not alike. c) The special destiny that the Lord designated for him: some have the fate of facing the trial of poverty, and some have the fate of facing the trial of wealth, and the like.

That is, the Lord created human beings different from one another and in conditions different from one another, because each person has his own destiny, so that together all human beings may reveal the word of the Lord and His blessing to the world. And it makes no difference whether this comes about through the constellations and stars or by other means; in any case, through individual Providence the Lord gives each person a mazal or a fate, through which he can add his special part to the rectification of the world. As the Sages said (Nidda 16b): "That angel who is appointed over conception… takes the drop and stands it before the Holy One, blessed be He, and says before Him: Master of the Universe, this drop, what will become of it? Mighty or weak? Wise or foolish? Rich or poor? But 'wicked or righteous' he did not say…." For the choice whether to be wicked or righteous is given into the hands of man, as it is stated (Devarim 10:12-13): "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you? Only to fear the Lord your God, to walk in all His ways and to love Him, and to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul; to keep the commandments of the Lord and His statutes which I command you this day for your good."

According to Rabbi Ḥanina, "Israel is subject to mazal"; that is, each person has his own fate, which provides a framework for his life, and within this framework he must strive to live in the best possible way and to increase Torah and mitzvot as far as he is able. And although sometimes, by virtue of Torah and mitzvot, the fate changes, generally it does not change, and therefore it is not proper to exert oneself to change it.

On the other hand, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, "Israel is not subject to mazal"; that is, although each person has his own fate, and generally it does not change, since Israel received the Torah, a person is able to change his mazal. Therefore, as a rule, it is not proper for a person to take mazal into account; rather, he should set the goals that seem proper in his eyes for the sake of Heaven and try to fulfil them, without fearing that mazal stands against him. As it is stated (Yirmiyahu 10:2): "Thus says the Lord: Do not learn the way of the nations, and do not be dismayed by the signs of the heavens, for the nations are dismayed by them" – "the nations will be dismayed, but not Israel." This is also the opinion of most of the Sages cited in the Talmud (Shabbat 156a), whose words were brought in the previous halakha.2

sections.title: It Is Forbidden to Ask Astrologers about the Future
sections.html:
It is forbidden to ask stargazers what will be in the future, and the Rishonim disagreed as to the severity of the prohibition. According to Rambam, one who consults stargazers transgresses the prohibitions of me'onen and menaḥesh, which are among the prohibitions of sorcery, as it is stated (Devarim 18:9-12): "When you come into the land that the Lord your God is giving you, you shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations. There shall not be found among you… a soothsayer, a diviner of omens or a sorcerer… For whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord." As Rabbi Akiva said (Sanhedrin 65b), a me'onen is "one who calculates times and hours, and says: Today is a good day to set out; tomorrow is a good day to buy." Likewise the Sages explained (ibid. 66a) the verse (Vayikra 19:26): "You shall not practise divination by omens, nor practise soothsaying" – "such as those who divine by means of a weasel, birds and stars." And since this involves a negative prohibition, if a person performed an action according to what they advised him, such as buying at the time they told him it was worthwhile to buy, he is liable to lashes (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:8-9; above 24:2).

According to Ramban, however, since the astrologers do not calculate the future by means of sorcery or divination but by way of wisdom, astrology does not involve the prohibition "You shall not practise divination by omens, nor practise soothsaying." Rather, it is forbidden to ask astrologers about the future because there is a mitzva to walk with the Lord in wholeheartedness, as the Sages said (Pesaḥim 113b): "From where do we know that one may not consult Chaldeans (stargazers)? As it is stated (Devarim 18:13): 'You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God.'" That is, one should not seek devices to know the future; rather, if the Lord reveals the future to us through a prophet or the Urim and Tumim – we will know it. And if not – we will rely on the Lord, that even if a distressing event befalls us, it is intended for our good. And if we find a device to know the future and evade that trouble, we will end up suffering many more troubles, for that trouble which is meant to come will in the end come in a more severe form. Therefore we have been commanded to conduct ourselves wholeheartedly with the Lord, and to accept with faith all the events that come upon us, and thereby we will grow and advance through them (above 19:12-13). However, the prohibition is to turn to the astrologers, but there is no prohibition to rely on their words. Therefore, if a person learned from astrologers whom he trusts that a certain thing is dangerous for him, and he fears it, he is permitted to refrain from doing it. And so it was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (SA and Rema YD 179:1-2).3

sections.title: Using an Astrologer for Personality Assessment
sections.html:
Having learned that it is forbidden to ask astrologers about the future, it remains to clarify whether a person may examine his personality with the help of an astrologer, in order to know what his principal traits are, which impulses he must beware of, and which talents he possesses and would do well to invest in developing.

Those who hold that there is no truth in astrology hold that it is forbidden to go for astrological counselling, because the Torah warned us to keep far from falsehood. For whoever follows false counsel deceives himself into thinking that he has traits that he does not have, or denies traits that he does have; and instead of exerting himself to develop his character according to his own understanding and according to what he hears from his teachers and friends, he will incline after vanities and neglect to develop his character and talents properly. Those who hold this view even bring proof from cases of people who, following such counselling, tended to invest in a certain direction that proved very harmful. For example, they were told that they had a talent for business, and in the end they lost all their property; or they heard that they had no talent for a certain field, and after many lost years it turned out that it was precisely in that field that they succeeded.

On the other hand, some say that a person may make use of astrology in order to deepen his understanding of his character and traits. For if he knows that he is liable to commit a certain sin, he can be on guard against it; and if he knows that he has a talent for a certain field, he can develop it further. This is in the manner of what the Sages said (Shabbat 156a) about one born under the mazal of Mars (Ma'adim), that by his nature he will tend to shed blood, but he can choose whether to be a murderer, a ritual slaughterer, a doctor or a mohel. Likewise the Sages related (Shabbat 156b) about the mother of Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, that astrologers told her that her son would be a thief. She took care that he would always have a head covering on his head, in order to arouse him to fear of Heaven. When he grew up, she asked him to always be careful to cover his head and to ask the Lord for mercy that the evil inclination should not rule over him. At first he did not understand why his mother was so worried. Once he was sitting and studying under a palm tree; the head covering fell from his head, he lifted his eyes to the palm tree and saw dates there; his inclination overcame him, and out of a great desire to steal he climbed the palm tree and tore off the cluster with his teeth. Then he understood his mother's worry. Thus, although the astrologers were mistaken and in practice Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak was not a thief, by virtue of their identifying his inclination to steal, his mother took care to educate him in the fear of Heaven, and thus he became one of the great Sages of Israel.

Yet one can still argue that in the past astrologers were of a high level, and there was room to take their words into account; but over the years their wisdom was forgotten and the mistakes in their words multiplied, and therefore today one should not consult them.

In practice, since the matter is disputed, it is preferable to follow the opinion of the stringent authorities, who forbid consulting an astrologer. And even one who wishes to rely on the opinion of the lenient authorities – since even according to them many err in this wisdom – should take care to go to an astrologer who is God-fearing, upright and humble, who is careful not to take decisive positions, and who is also endowed with educational understanding.4

sections.title: Physiognomy and Palm Reading
sections.html:
Physiognomy (ḥokhmat ha-partzuf) is based on the assumption that there is a correspondence between the soul and the body, and therefore the shape of the body, and especially the face, which is the principal expression of a person, expresses his character and fate. Similarly, palm reading is based on the assumption that since a person performs all his deeds with his hands, the shape of his hand and the lines on it express his character and fate.

The Sages of Israel too agreed that there is profound wisdom in this, as explained in the Zohar (part 2, 78a), that Yitro proposed to Moshe our teacher to appoint judges who would bear with him the burden of the people according to physiognomy. They learned this from the verse (Shemot 18:21): "And you shall behold out of all the people capable men, God-fearing, men of truth, hating unjust gain, and place them over them as officers of thousands, officers of hundreds, officers of fifties and officers of tens." He did not say "and you shall choose" but "and you shall behold," meaning that by means of physiognomy he would choose the suitable judges. However, Moshe our teacher did not need this, but made use of the holy spirit. Similarly, it is brought in the responsa of the Ge'onim, from Rav Sherira Gaon and Rav Hai Gaon, that the Sages used this wisdom, and taught the secrets of the Torah only to one whom they saw, by means of physiognomy, to be suitable for it (Sha'arei Teshuva 122). So too wrote Ramban, but he added that following the destruction and the exile, "when we were lost, the branches of wisdom were lost with us, and their memory remained in a corrupted form in the hands of a few, and the philosophers came and denied them" (Derasha Torat Hashem Temima, Bereshit 5:2 [?]). That is, since the precise tradition of this wisdom was lost, this wisdom remained corrupted, and consequently, when the philosophers examined it, they found it mistaken.

Likewise, Rabbi Ḥayim Vital testified concerning the holy Ari that, being possessed of the holy spirit, he also knew how to read palms, but did not wish to teach this wisdom because he regarded it as a "foreign wisdom" (Shivḥei Ha-Ari, p. 22). It seems that physiognomy and palm reading relied on an inspiration that is a kind of prophecy; and when we passed from the era of prophecy to the era of wisdom, inspiration diminished, and the sages became accustomed to examine everything in a defined and detailed way, and found it difficult to learn and teach a wisdom that relies on inspiration. And since they invested less in studying it, corruptions in it multiplied. The Ari knew it with the help of the holy spirit, but did not wish to teach it, because he knew that without the holy spirit it would remain a "foreign" and corrupted wisdom.

After all this, in practice the attitude to physiognomy and palm reading is like the attitude to astrology. Some say that it is forbidden to make use of these branches of wisdom because of the prohibition of "you shall not practise soothsaying," which also includes a prohibition to foretell the future and to plan actions according to these methods and the like (Leḥem Mishneh, according to the view of Rambam). On the other hand, some say that there is no prohibition in using these branches of wisdom, because they do not involve sorcery; but the permission is on condition that one goes to someone who truly understands them, whereas in practice most of those who engage in these branches of wisdom frequently err.

The main opinion of most of the Sages of Israel is that this does not involve the prohibition of "you shall not practise soothsaying," but because of the mitzva of "You shall be wholehearted" it is forbidden to seek hidden things and the future by obscure means. In addition, one should also not rely on these branches of wisdom, since even when they are accurate they reflect the person's present nature and situation, whereas a person can change his nature and fate through his choices. Admittedly, there is apparently no prohibition in ascertaining one's character by means of them; but in practice, even for this purpose it is better not to resort to them, because it is very difficult to arrive at the truth through them. And even if one succeeds in seeing some of the traits through them, any mistake could cause great confusion. For this is not like a rabbi who knows his student, or a psychologist who talks with his patient, whose advice rests on reason, so that the student or patient can examine their advice with his own intellect. But when the advice is given by branches of wisdom whose ways are obscure, it is difficult for a person to reject their mistaken analysis through reason, and his life may become entangled as a result. For example, he may think that he has a certain talent and choose a certain profession in order to realise it, whereas in truth he has a different talent.5
